OUTPUT   data/processed/nhanes_clean.csv    all 11,933 participants, 485 variables

## Data preprocessing

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source(here::here("R", "utils.R"))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5, dpi = 150,
                      dev = c("png", "cairo_pdf"),
                      fig.path = file.path(paths$figures, "02_preprocessing", ""))
```

```{r load}
nhanes_raw <- load_raw_data()
codebook   <- load_codebook()
```

### Creating a working dataset
Based on the findings of the exploratory analysis, several preprocessing decisions were made to prepare the dataset for subsequent analyses.

A separate working dataset was created to ensure that the original NHANES dataset remains unchanged. General preprocessing steps will be applied to this working dataset, whereas analysis-specific preprocessing will be performed separately in Parts 2, 3 and 4.

```{r}
nhanes <- nhanes_raw
nhanes_clean <- nhanes
```

### Recoding special response codes
As identified during the exploratory analysis, certain categorical variables contain special response codes representing "Refused" or "Don't know". These codes do not represent valid categories for the characteristics being investigated.

The confirmed special response codes for education level (`DMDEDUC2`) and marital status (`DMDMARTZ`) were therefore recoded as `NA`. Recoding was performed on a variable-specific basis to avoid replacing valid numerical observations.


```{r}
nhanes_clean <- nhanes_clean %>%
  mutate(
    DMDEDUC2 = if_else(
      DMDEDUC2 %in% c(7, 9),
      NA_real_,
      DMDEDUC2
    ),
    DMDMARTZ = if_else(
      DMDMARTZ %in% c(77, 99),
      NA_real_,
      DMDMARTZ
    )
  )
```

```{r}
# Education level
table(nhanes$DMDEDUC2, useNA = "ifany")
table(nhanes_clean$DMDEDUC2, useNA = "ifany")

# Marital status
table(nhanes$DMDMARTZ, useNA = "ifany")
table(nhanes_clean$DMDMARTZ, useNA = "ifany")
```

A total of 11 education responses and nine marital status responses were recoded as missing values. The remaining valid categories were retained. This ensures that these special response codes are not incorrectly treated as meaningful categories during subsequent analyses.

Additional special response codes will be evaluated when the corresponding variables are selected for further analyses.

### Handling uninformative variables
The exploratory analysis identified one completely missing variable, `BMIHEAD`. Since this variable contains no observed information, it was removed from the working dataset.

Variables with only one unique non-missing value were retained at this stage, as some of them contain information related to measurement quality or study design. Their suitability as analysis features will be evaluated separately.

```{r}
# Identify completely missing variables
all_missing_vars <- names(nhanes_clean)[
  colSums(!is.na(nhanes_clean)) == 0
]

all_missing_vars
```

```{r}
# Remove completely missing variables
nhanes_clean <- nhanes_clean %>%
  select(-all_of(all_missing_vars))
```

```{r}
# Compare dimensions
dim(nhanes)
dim(nhanes_clean)
```

After removing the completely missing variable, the working dataset contains 11,933 participants and 485 variables. No participants were removed during this preprocessing step.

### Handling categorical variables 
Several demographic variables are stored numerically despite representing categorical information. To ensure that these variables are interpreted correctly during subsequent statistical analyses, selected nominal variables were converted into factors, while education level was converted into an ordered factor.

Continuous measurements and quantitative variables were retained in their original numerical format.

```{r}
nhanes_clean <- nhanes_clean %>%
  mutate(
    RIAGENDR = factor(
      RIAGENDR,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),

    RIDSTATR = factor(
      RIDSTATR,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Interview only", "Examined")
    ),

    RIDRETH3 = factor(
      RIDRETH3,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7),
      labels = c(
        "Mexican American",
        "Other Hispanic",
        "Non-Hispanic White",
        "Non-Hispanic Black",
        "Non-Hispanic Asian",
        "Other race"
      )
    ),

    DMDEDUC2 = factor(
      DMDEDUC2,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
      labels = c(
        "Less than 9th grade",
        "9th-11th grade",
        "High school graduate",
        "Some college",
        "College graduate or above"
      ),
      ordered = TRUE
    ),

    DMDMARTZ = factor(
      DMDMARTZ,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Married or living with partner",
        "Widowed, divorced or separated",
        "Never married"
        )
)
  )
```

#### Checking the conversion 

```{r}
str(nhanes_clean %>%
      select(RIAGENDR, RIDSTATR, RIDRETH3,
             DMDEDUC2, DMDMARTZ))
```

```{r}
table(nhanes_clean$RIAGENDR, useNA = "ifany")
table(nhanes_clean$RIDSTATR, useNA = "ifany")
table(nhanes_clean$RIDRETH3, useNA = "ifany")
table(nhanes_clean$DMDEDUC2, useNA = "ifany")
table(nhanes_clean$DMDMARTZ, useNA = "ifany")
```

```{r}
categorical_vars <- c(
  "RIAGENDR", "RIDSTATR", "RIDRETH3",
  "DMDEDUC2", "DMDMARTZ"
)

data.frame(
  variable = categorical_vars,
  missing_before = colSums(
    is.na(nhanes[categorical_vars])
  ),
  missing_after = colSums(
    is.na(nhanes_clean[categorical_vars])
  )
)
```

The selected demographic variables were successfully converted into factors, with education level represented as an ordered factor. The number of missing values remained unchanged, except for the previously recoded special response codes in education level and marital status.

This indicates that the conversion did not introduce additional missing values.

### Handling missing values
The exploratory analysis demonstrated that a substantial proportion of missing values is related to the NHANES study design, including examination participation and age-dependent eligibility.

Therefore, no global imputation or complete-case filtering was performed. Applying these methods to the entire dataset could introduce inappropriate values or unnecessarily exclude participants with missing information for variables that are not relevant to a particular analysis.

Instead, missing values will be handled separately for each subsequent analysis, depending on the selected variables, study population and statistical method.

### Handling outliers and top-coded values
Potential outliers identified during the exploratory analysis were retained because extreme clinical measurements may reflect genuine biological variation or pathological conditions rather than measurement errors.

Top-coded observations were also retained, as these values represent valid observations with limited numerical precision.

Similarly, laboratory values below the limit of detection were retained as provided by NHANES. The corresponding comment codes will be considered when evaluating the suitability of individual laboratory variables for subsequent analyses.

No general outlier removal or additional substitution of values below the detection limit was performed.

### Handling redundant variables 
The exploratory analysis identified several sources of potentially redundant information, including measurements expressed in different units, repeated clinical measurements and strongly correlated biological variables.

These variables were retained in the general working dataset, as their relevance depends on the objectives of subsequent analyses.

When selecting features for individual analyses, duplicate representations of the same measurement will be avoided. Strong correlations between biologically distinct variables will be evaluated in the context of the statistical model rather than used as an automatic exclusion criterion.

### Transformations and scaling
Although several continuous variables showed right-skewed distributions, no general logarithmic transformation or standardization was applied to the working dataset.

The need for transformation depends on the distribution of individual variables and the assumptions of the selected statistical method. Furthermore, for machine learning applications, preprocessing parameters such as means and standard deviations should be estimated from the training data only to prevent data leakage.

Transformations and scaling will therefore be performed separately when required by subsequent analyses.

### Shared analysis population
In line with the decision above, no participants are removed. However, Parts 2, 3 and 4 all analyse examination and laboratory measurements in adults, and they should do so in exactly the same group of people, so that sample sizes and results can be compared between parts. This group is therefore defined once, here, as a flag (`analysis_population`) instead of a filter:

- examined participants (`RIDSTATR`), because only they have examination and laboratory data;
- aged 20 years or older, because several adult variables, such as education level, are only collected from age 20;
- not pregnant at examination (`RIDEXPRG` = 1 excluded), because pregnancy changes body measurements such as waist circumference and blood measurements such as HbA1c. Participants whose pregnancy status could not be determined (`RIDEXPRG` = 3) are kept.

```{r analysis-population}
nhanes_clean <- nhanes_clean %>%
  mutate(
    analysis_population = RIDSTATR == "Examined" &
      RIDAGEYR >= 20 &
      (is.na(RIDEXPRG) | RIDEXPRG != 1)
  )

tibble(
  step = c("All participants", "Examined", "Aged 20 years or older",
           "Not pregnant (analysis population)"),
  n = c(
    nrow(nhanes_clean),
    sum(nhanes_clean$RIDSTATR == "Examined"),
    sum(nhanes_clean$RIDSTATR == "Examined" & nhanes_clean$RIDAGEYR >= 20),
    sum(nhanes_clean$analysis_population)
  )
)
```

Later parts select this group with `filter(analysis_population)` and then handle missing values for their own variables only.

### Variable information for later parts
To make the feature selection in later parts consistent and reproducible, the variable classification from the exploratory analysis is stored together with three properties per variable:

- `unit_duplicate`: the same measurement reported a second time in another unit. These are detected as two measurement variables from the same NHANES file whose labels are identical apart from the unit in brackets; the first one is kept as the primary version.
- `pct_missing` and `pct_missing_analysis`: the percentage of missing values in all participants and in the analysis population.
- `pct_below_lod`: the percentage of values below the limit of detection in the analysis population, linked from the corresponding laboratory comment code.

No transformation is decided here (`transform` = "none"), in line with the decision to transform per analysis.

```{r variable-info}
# Same classification rules as in 01_exploration
ordinal_vars  <- c("DMDEDUC2", "DMDHREDZ", "DMDHSEDZ", "DMDHRAGZ", "ALQ121", "ALQ142", "ALQ270", "ALQ280",
                   "BPAOCSZ", "BMDBMIC", "WHQ030E", "DBQ390", "DBQ421", "DBQ424", "RIDEXMON", "DMDYRUSR")
discrete_vars <- c("RIDAGEYR", "RIDAGEMN", "RIDEXAGM", "DMDHHSIZ", "ALQ130", "ALQ170", "DBD381", "DBD411",
                   "ECD070A", "ECD070B", "DBD030", "DBD041", "DBD050", "DBD055", "DBD061")

analysis_data <- nhanes_clean %>% filter(analysis_population)

variable_info <- codebook %>%
  filter(variable %in% names(nhanes_clean)) %>%
  mutate(
    position = match(variable, names(nhanes_clean)),
    n_unique = sapply(nhanes_clean[variable], function(x) length(unique(na.omit(x)))),
    type = case_when(
      variable == "SEQN" ~ "identifier",
      grepl("^WT", variable) | variable %in% c("SDMVSTRA", "SDMVPSU", "SDDSRVYR") ~ "survey design / weight",
      grepl("comment|comt|cmt", label, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "comment code",
      variable %in% ordinal_vars ~ "ordinal",
      variable %in% discrete_vars ~ "discrete",
      !sapply(nhanes_clean[variable], is.numeric) | n_unique <= 12 ~ "nominal",
      TRUE ~ "continuous"
    ),
    base_label = str_trim(str_remove(label, "\\s*\\([^()]*\\)\\s*$")),
    pct_missing = sapply(nhanes_clean[variable], function(x) mean(is.na(x)) * 100),
    pct_missing_analysis = sapply(analysis_data[variable], function(x) mean(is.na(x)) * 100)
  ) %>%
  # FASTQX_L is excluded: there "(hours)" and "(minutes)" are two parts of one duration
  group_by(file, base_label) %>%
  mutate(unit_duplicate = type %in% c("continuous", "discrete") & file != "FASTQX_L" &
           row_number() > 1) %>%
  ungroup()

# Link every laboratory comment code to its measurement: the nearest preceding
# measurement variable in the same NHANES file.
comment_codes <- variable_info %>%
  filter(type == "comment code", component == "Laboratory")
measurements <- variable_info %>%
  filter(type %in% c("continuous", "discrete"), !unit_duplicate)

lod_link <- comment_codes %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(measured = {
    candidates <- measurements[measurements$file == file & measurements$position < position, ]
    if (nrow(candidates) == 0) NA_character_ else candidates$variable[which.max(candidates$position)]
  }) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  transmute(variable = measured,
            pct_below_lod = sapply(analysis_data[comment_codes$variable],
                                   function(x) mean(x == 1, na.rm = TRUE) * 100))

variable_info <- variable_info %>%
  left_join(lod_link, by = "variable") %>%
  mutate(transform = "none", offset = 0) %>%
  select(variable, label, file, component, type, unit_duplicate,
         pct_missing, pct_missing_analysis, pct_below_lod, transform, offset)

count(variable_info, type)
sum(variable_info$unit_duplicate)
variable_info %>%
  filter(!is.na(pct_below_lod)) %>%
  summarise(lab_tests_with_lod = n(), more_than_half_below_lod = sum(pct_below_lod > 50))
```

### Summary of preprocessing decision

| Data quality issue | Preprocessing decision |
|---|---|
| Original dataset | Retained unchanged |
| Special response codes | Confirmed invalid codes in selected variables recoded as NA |
| Completely missing variables | Removed |
| Constant variables | Retained |
| Categorical variables | Selected variables converted into factors |
| Missing values | No global imputation or participant exclusion |
| Potential outliers | Retained |
| Top-coded values | Retained |
| Values below the LOD | Retained as provided by NHANES |
| Redundant variables | Retained |
| Transformations and scaling | Deferred to subsequent analyses |
| Analysis population | Flagged (examined, aged 20 years or older, not pregnant); no participants removed |
| Variable information | Type, unit duplicates, missingness and % below the LOD stored in `variable_info.csv` |

General preprocessing addressed confirmed data quality issues while preserving the available biological and clinical information. No research question-specific participant or feature selection was performed. Further preprocessing will depend on the objectives and statistical requirements of subsequent analyses.

## Quality control after preprocessing
The preprocessing should only change what was intended. Three checks confirm this: the participants are the same, only the recoded variables gained missing values, and every other variable is unchanged.

```{r qc}
# Same participants, in the same order
identical(nhanes_raw$SEQN, nhanes_clean$SEQN)

# Variables that were intentionally changed or added
changed_vars <- c("DMDEDUC2", "DMDMARTZ", "RIAGENDR", "RIDSTATR", "RIDRETH3")
added_vars   <- "analysis_population"
removed_vars <- setdiff(names(nhanes_raw), names(nhanes_clean))
removed_vars

# All other variables are identical to the raw data
unchanged_vars <- setdiff(names(nhanes_clean), c(changed_vars, added_vars))
all(sapply(unchanged_vars, function(v) identical(nhanes_raw[[v]], nhanes_clean[[v]])))

# Extra missing values come only from the recoded special response codes
tibble(
  variable = changed_vars,
  missing_raw = colSums(is.na(nhanes_raw[changed_vars])),
  missing_clean = colSums(is.na(nhanes_clean[changed_vars]))
)
```

## Summary and suitability for further analysis
The working dataset contains all 11,933 participants and 485 of the 486 original variables, plus the `analysis_population` flag. Confirmed special response codes were recoded, the completely missing variable was removed and key demographic variables were converted to factors. All other values are identical to the raw data.

The dataset is suitable for the subsequent analyses, provided that each part:

- selects the shared analysis population with `filter(analysis_population)`;
- chooses its variables with `variable_info.csv`, keeping one version of each unit duplicate and taking the proportion below the LOD into account;
- handles missing values, transformations and scaling for its own variables, and reports how.

## Save the clean dataset
A CSV file does not store factor levels; `load_clean_data()` in `R/utils.R` restores them when the data are read back in.

```{r save}
dir.create(dirname(paths$clean_data), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(nhanes_clean, paths$clean_data)
write_csv(variable_info, paths$clean_vars)

dim(nhanes_clean)
```
